demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette: Sara is a 75-year-old judge from a Middle Eastern background who has been navigating the aftermath of losing her husband, Muhammad, to an unexpected heart attack six months ago. Sara and Muhammad had been married for over fifty years, and his sudden death has left her reeling with grief and a sense of profound loss. In the weeks following Muhammad's passing, Sara experienced vivid flashbacks that brought back memories of their final moments together. She often finds herself at work, lost in thought, replaying the last conversation they had. The day was uneventful; she remembers him saying how proud he was of her work and how much he loved her. Those words echo through her mind now, punctuated by a sharp pain every time she thinks about his sudden departure. Sara's days are filled with moments where she feels acutely aware that Muhammad is no longer there to share them with her. She wakes up each morning to the silence of an empty house, which was once filled with their shared laughter and conversations. Sara often finds herself checking if Muhammad has left a note or missed an appointment on his planner, only to remember he's gone. As a judge, Sara's work requires focus and composure, but she struggles to maintain her usual level of concentration. She reports feeling easily distracted by intrusive thoughts about her husband. During court sessions, she often finds herself drifting off, thinking about the times they would discuss cases over dinner or how he would always reassure her that she was making a difference in people's lives. Sara has also started having nightmares where Muhammad is still alive, and they are sharing one last meal together, only to be abruptly woken up by the reality of his absence. These dreams leave her feeling disoriented and anxious each morning. She often wakes up drenched in sweat, replaying the dream over and over again until she can convince herself that it was just a dream. Recently, Sara has been avoiding places where they used to go together, like their favorite restaurant or the park where they would take long walks. These avoidance behaviors have extended beyond physical locations; she avoids watching television shows they both enjoyed because it brings up too many painful memories and triggers her anxiety. Sara's relationships with her children have become strained as well. She feels guilty about spending time with them, thinking that Muhammad wouldn't want her to be happy without him. This guilt is compounded by the sense of emptiness she feels when she thinks about how much Muhammad would enjoy seeing his grandchildren grow up. At home, Sara has taken to watching old home videos of her and Muhammad together. Initially, she found some solace in these memories, but now they serve as a stark reminder of what she's lost. She often cries while watching them, feeling overwhelmed by the contrast between those joyful moments and the current void in her life. Sara's social activities have dwindled significantly since his death. She used to be part of a weekly book club, but she has stopped attending meetings because the idea of sitting through an entire evening without Muhammad feels unbearable. Her friends have noticed the change and express concern, but Sara finds it difficult to open up about her grief. Sara's PTSD symptoms are woven into the fabric of her daily life, affecting not only her personal relationships but also her professional responsibilities as a judge. She continues to work diligently, driven by a sense of duty and routine, but the emotional toll is significant. Despite her resilience, Sara often wonders how she will continue to navigate this new reality without Muhammad at her side. Her days are marked by moments of profound sadness interspersed with flashes of anger directed at herself for feeling so lost. She knows she needs support but struggles to reach out, fearing that admitting vulnerability might make the pain even more real.
